#1 This may just show my ignorance, but I am wondering how to see the following:

 \,

For k∈N>0k \in \mathbb{N}_{\gt 0}k∈N>0​ and a∈Na \in \mathbb{N}a∈N, the expression

Sk(a) ≔ ∑n=0k−1eπik(n+a)2 S_k(a) \,\coloneqq\, \sum_{n = 0}^{k-1} e^{ \tfrac{\pi \mathrm{i}}{k} (n + a)^2 } Sk​(a):=n=0∑k−1​ekπi​(n+a)2

is independent of aaa if kkk is even:

k  is even      ⇒      ∀a(  Sk(a)=Sk(0)  ) . k\;\text{is even} \;\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;\; \underset{a}{\forall} \big( \; S_k(a) = S_k(0) \; \big) \,. kis even⇒a∀​(Sk​(a)=Sk​(0)).

In a roundabout way this follows from the modular transformation law of conformal characters of the U(1)\mathrm{U}(1)U(1) WZW model.

But what’s an elementary arithmetic way to see this?

(If the exponent had another factor of “2”, then it would follow easily, also for odd kkk, by modular arithmetic, now in the other sense of “modular”. But the question is for the exponent as given.)
subject: a trig identity

#5 Right, so the summands are kkk-periodic after all, because

eπik(n+k)2  =  eπik(n2+2nk+k2)  =  eπikn2eπi(2n+k)⏟1  if  k  even  =  eπikn2 e^{ \tfrac{\pi \mathrm{i}}{k} (n + k)^2 } \;=\; e^{ \tfrac{\pi \mathrm{i}}{k} (n^2 + 2 n k + k^2) } \;=\; e^{ \tfrac{\pi \mathrm{i}}{k} n^2 } \underset{ 1\;\mathrm{if}\;k\;\mathrm{even} }{ \underbrace{ e^{ \pi \mathrm{i}(2n + k) } } } \;=\; e^{ \tfrac{\pi \mathrm{i}}{k} n^2 } ekπi​(n+k)2=ekπi​(n2+2nk+k2)=ekπi​n21ifkeveneπi(2n+k)​​=ekπi​n2

and so if we shift n↦n+an \mapsto n + an↦n+a in the exponent, then we may just relabel to get rid of the aaa.

Thanks! :-)

If in my construction of irreps of Z2^⋊SL2(Z)\widehat{\mathbb{Z}^2} \rtimes {\mathrm{SL}}_2(\mathbb{Z})Z2⋊SL2​(Z) (here) I replace the factor

ζ ≔ eπik \zeta \,\coloneqq\, e^{ \tfrac{\pi \mathrm{i}}{k} } ζ:=ekπi​

throughout by eπikqe^{ \tfrac{\pi \mathrm{i}}{k}q }ekπi​q, for q∈{1,2,⋯ ,k−1}q \in \{1,2, \cdots, k-1\}q∈{1,2,⋯,k−1}, then all conclusions seem to remain valid.

Indeed, it seems to me that if qqq is chosen to be even, then we no longer need to assume that kkk is even, because the analogue of the above periodicity of summands (used here) follows already as

eπikq(n+k)2  =  eπikq(n2+2nk+k2)  =  eπikqn2eπiq(2n+k)⏟1  since  q  even  =  eπikqn2 e^{ \tfrac{\pi \mathrm{i}}{k}q (n + k)^2 } \;=\; e^{ \tfrac{\pi \mathrm{i}}{k}q (n^2 + 2 n k + k^2) } \;=\; e^{ \tfrac{\pi \mathrm{i}}{k}q n^2 } \underset{ 1\;\mathrm{since}\;q\;\mathrm{even} }{ \underbrace{ e^{ \pi \mathrm{i}q(2n + k) } } } \;=\; e^{ \tfrac{\pi \mathrm{i}}{k} q n^2 }ekπi​q(n+k)2=ekπi​q(n2+2nk+k2)=ekπi​qn21sinceqeveneπiq(2n+k)​​=ekπi​qn2

This is not a contradiction in itself, but it does seem to be in contradiction to Will Sawin’s reply to me on MO here, where he seems to exclude such irreps of odd kkk. I must again be missing something.

and
